connector: Uncle Henrik comes home from his boat and talks about the weather for fishing. Then he tells the girls that Great-aunt Birte has died. Annemarie has heard every story about her mother’s family, and she has never heard that name. As you read, notice what the grown-ups say, and what they leave out.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Grete. Uncle Henrik comes home from the sea, and something isn’t quite right. A relative nobody has ever mentioned has died, and there will be a casket in the living room. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 8, and draft more of your essay. Today’s question: what is really going on at Uncle Henrik’s house?
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move asks you to weigh courage. When several people are brave in the same chapter, ask what each one could lose. A grown-up and a child might both be brave, but the cost isn’t always the same. Look for the details that show you what’s at stake.
transcripts.dol: The model is a short sentence about Uncle Henrik. The sentence to fix is about a name nobody recognizes. That name has a title in front of it, and the title needs capitals and a small joining mark. And again, two sentences need to be split apart.
transcripts.guide1: This is review, so some of what you see is already right. In grammar and spelling, only tap what needs fixing. Read every line twice before you decide. A good editor knows when to change something, and also when to leave it alone.
transcripts.morphology: This is the last stretch of water. Four more words, and the beam can finally reach the far shore. One of these words describes someone who believes things too easily. As you read, ask whether anyone in this chapter is hoping someone will believe a story.
transcripts.vocabulary: Last match of the week. See if you can do it with no misses at all. Then try something harder: use two of the words together in one sentence about Annemarie at the house by the sea. Discreet and tense might make a good pair.
transcripts.grammar: Here’s a little draft with some mistakes and some sentences that are fine. Read each one quietly to yourself. Your ear usually knows before your brain can name the rule. Tap only the sentences that sound wrong, then fix one of them.
transcripts.spelling: Six built words, and only some are misspelled. For each one, take it apart: the base, the piece at the front, the piece at the end. Then check each part on its own. Usually only one part has gone wrong.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about keeping quiet. Annemarie can tell something about this family story doesn’t add up. She doesn’t argue. She watches. When I was a girl, I learned that sometimes the bravest person in the room is a child who notices everything and says nothing until it’s safe.
transcripts.read: Uncle Henrik is a fisherman, and he talks a lot about the weather. Listen to the phrases he uses. Have you heard one of them before? Then pay close attention near the end of the chapter, when Annemarie hears a name she doesn’t know. Notice what she thinks, and what she says out loud.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The questions ask why the news of a death seems strange, what an odd phrase about fishing might mean, and what Annemarie begins to suspect. Then you’ll draft a second body paragraph, with a new reason and a new piece of evidence.
transcripts.chapter: For the second question, think back to the phone call in Chapter 6. Where else have you heard grown-ups talk about fishing weather? You don’t have to be sure what it means. A good guess, backed up by what you noticed, is exactly what a careful reader does.
transcripts.workshop: Two reasons are stronger than one. This paragraph has the same shape as the last one: reason, evidence, link. But it needs a brand-new reason and a brand-new quote. If your two paragraphs sound the same, look for a different moment in the book.

a.raw: annemarie does not know who great aunt birte is the name is unfamiliar to her
a.fixed: Annemarie does not know who Great-Aunt Birte is. The name is unfamiliar to her.
a.why: A capital A on Annemarie, capitals and a hyphen on Great-Aunt Birte, a period after is, a capital T to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: uncle henrik picks up the kitten he says great aunt birte has died
b.fixed: Uncle Henrik picks up the kitten. He says Great-Aunt Birte has died.
b.why: Capitals on Uncle Henrik, a period after kitten, a capital H to start the second sentence, capitals and a hyphen on Great-Aunt Birte, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain how Annemarie’s love of her mother’s stories helps her notice.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain why the grown-ups would need a code at all.
scholar.journal-q3: … and explain why Annemarie says nothing about what she suspects.

match.intend: Intend has the root that means stretch. Look for the meaning about planning to do something on purpose.
match.credible: Credible has the root that means believe. Look for the meaning about being easy to believe.
match.discreet: Discreet is about being careful and quiet. Look for the meaning about not drawing attention.
match.tense: Tense is a feeling in your body. Look for the meaning about being tight with worry.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Each stretching word reaches the light across the water; each believing word lights a window on the far shore.

why.t: In Chapter 7, Annemarie stands on the shore at Gilleleje and points across the sea to Sweden. tend means to stretch, so each right tend word stretches the lighthouse beam a little farther across the water. cred means to believe, so each right cred word lights a window on the far shore. One stretch of water each lesson, until the light reaches Sweden.

miss.fill1: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is credulous about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill2: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is creditor about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill3: Not quite. cred means believe. Is tendency about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill4: Not quite. cred means believe. Is superintendent about believing, or about stretching?

wordgame.win: The light reaches all the way across the water, and on the far shore, Kullen’s lighthouse answers. cred = believe, tend = stretch.

notes.wgrd: Not every brave act costs the same. List who is brave, ask what each one could lose, and use the book’s words to explain who risks the most.
vocab: To plan to do something on purpose.
notes.wordParts: cred means “to believe” (credible, incredible). tend means “to stretch” or “to reach” (extend, pretend, attend).
notes.grammar: A pronoun and its verb must agree. With he, she or it, the verb takes an s: she watches, he listens. With I, you, we or they, it doesn’t: they wait.
notes.spelling: Many long words are built from parts: a prefix in front (un-, re-, dis-), a base word, and a suffix at the end (-ful, -ly, -ness, -ance). Find the base underneath and keep its spelling: hope + ful + ly = hopefully.

case.title: A Boat That Crossed
case.alt: A small wooden boat with a red and white hull and a little cabin, displayed in a dim museum hall.
label: This small wooden boat is now in the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C. In October 1943 it carried Jewish refugees from Denmark across the water to Sweden, twelve to fourteen people on each trip.
Hundreds of Danish boats made crossings like this that autumn. Many belonged to fishermen, who knew the water, the weather and the currents better than anyone.

look.q: How many people do you think could fit inside this boat?
look.a: About twelve to fourteen on each trip, squeezed in tight and keeping very still.

look.q: Why would a fishing boat going out to sea not look strange?
look.a: Fishermen went out every day. A fishing boat on the water was the most ordinary sight on the coast.
